unchecked.text: Napoleon has deliberately given up the Pratzen plateau and left his right, along the lower Goldbach, looking thin enough to invite attack. Weyrother's Allied orders, read out at Krzenowitz after midnight to commanders who largely did not understand them, send four of five columns south-west across the French front. Fog fills the Goldbach valley. Soult's two assault divisions are standing in it, invisible from the heights.

Ten kilometres of open Moravian farmland. The French army, marked in blue, is to the west; to the east are the Russians and the Austrians, marked in amber. Between them runs the Goldbach, a small stream in its valley, and behind it stands the Pratzen plateau, the high ground in the centre of the field.
At about a quarter to nine Saint-Hilaire and Vandamme climb out of the fog onto a plateau the Allies are leaving. Two divisions, the Guard held back, against a column still filing off the heights.

With the plateau gone the Allied army is in two halves that can no longer help one another. Buxhowden's columns are still attacking westward and will not learn what has happened behind them until about noon.

The French centre turns ninety degrees and comes down off the heights into the rear of the Allied left. A way out for them is the neck of dry ground at Augezd, under guns on ground the Allies held at dawn.

Weyrother's orders send four of the five Allied columns south-west, off the plateau, to turn the French right and cut the road to Vienna. The heavy arrows are the intended lines of march. Note what they all have in common: they lead away from the centre.

Napoleon gave up the plateau on 1 December and camped behind the Goldbach, leaving his right so thin that a single division held five kilometres of stream. The weakness was real, which is what made it convincing.

In this model's terrain an observer on the Pratzeberg summit can see about 73 per cent of the field, and one on the valley floor at Puntowitz under 3 per cent. That is a reading from the model, not a record of what anyone saw: on the morning of the battle the valley lay in fog, and it was the fog that hid Soult's divisions forming at the foot of the slope.

Kienmayer's Austrian advance guard attacks Telnitz, the southernmost village on the Goldbach. Legrand's thin line holds the buildings and the vineyard bank above them, and the village changes hands repeatedly. Behind Kienmayer, Dokhturov's I Column is coming down off the southern end of the plateau.

Langeron and Przybyszewski attack Sokolnitz village, its castle and the pheasantry beyond. On the plateau the 4th Column, which was meant to replace the troops leaving the heights, is still standing still: Liechtenstein's cavalry has cut across its line of march. A gap opens between it and the 3rd Column.

Saint-Hilaire and Vandamme climb out of the fog into sunlight onto a plateau the 4th Column is still crossing. Saint-Hilaire makes for the Pratzeberg south of Pratzen village, Vandamme for Stare Vinohrady, the 'old vineyards', north-east of the village. Kutuzov, riding with the 4th Column, sees the danger and begins pulling troops back. The Allied centre is being broken, but the plateau will not be firmly French until about 11:00.

Kamensky's brigade, marching for Sokolnitz at the tail of Langeron's column, sees the French on the height behind it, turns about and attacks. Jurczek's Austrians join in and Saint-Hilaire is pushed back toward the crest. In the same hour, and independently, Lannes begins his advance astride the Olmütz highway in the north.

Liechtenstein's and Uvarov's horse charge the French cavalry screen and Murat answers with Nansouty's and d'Hautpoul's cuirassiers. The Santon and its eighteen guns hold the flank, Blasowitz falls; in Thiers, Lannes then carries Holubitz and Krug and parts Bagration's infantry from Liechtenstein's cavalry, while in Schönhals Bagration's line is broken later, by Caffarelli's, Suchet's and d'Hautpoul's attacks. On the plateau, Saint-Hilaire's brigades carry their part of the Pratzen heights with their own charge, as Thiébault tells it, and Schönhals has Soult send Levasseur's brigade to support their right.

With the plateau secure and the Allied right pushed back beyond Blasowitz, Napoleon turns his centre ninety degrees. Saint-Hilaire and Vandamme come down off the heights onto the back of Buxhowden's three columns, supported by the Guard and the grenadier division, while Davout resumes the offensive from the west. Przybyszewski's column, caught between them in Sokolnitz, is surrounded.

knew / doc / That Blasowitz had fallen.
knew / doc / That Buxhowden's columns were still fighting in the villages, unaware of what had happened behind them.

ordered / inf / A retreat of the left. No order of the day naming its route has been read (the disposition's retreat for the left ran by the Turas wood, Kobelnitz and Puntowitz); that it went south over the Augezd defile and the meres is inferred from the accounts of the end (Schönhals).

knew / inf / That the way out by Augezd came under artillery fire from the height (Schönhals's 'auf der Höhe'; that it is the height above Augezd, ground the army had held at dawn, is this map's reading); what the command knew of it is inferred.
c. 01:00 / Weyrother reads the dispositions at Allied headquarters, Krzenowitz. Kutuzov reportedly dozes.
c. 08:00 / Langeron attacks Sokolnitz; Przybyszewski goes for the castle and pheasantry.
c. 08:45 / Soult's divisions advance. The mist lifts off the heights.
c. 09:00 / Thiébault's brigade clears Pratzen village; the 10e Légère pushes on for the Pratzeberg.
c. 09:30 / Lannes advances along the highway. Bagration counter-attacks. The two battles now run in parallel.
c. 10:40 / The cavalry collision west of Blasowitz. Kellermann falls back through his infantry and reforms.
c. 11:00 / The Pratzeberg is firmly in French hands.
c. 12:00 / Napoleon moves forward from the Zuran to Stare Vinohrady.
c. 12:00 / Buxhowden, on the Allied left, is still unaware of the collapse behind him.

c. 12:30 / Davout regroups and attacks; Langeron is forced back toward Sokolnitz, in this map's reading, which no account read gives. The hour is this map's; Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky has Napoleon order the attack at one in the afternoon.
c. 13:00-14:00 / Soult and Davout launch the converging assault on the Allied left.
c. 14:00 / Sokolnitz falls. Przybyszewski's column is broken up and largely captured.
c. 14:30 / Vandamme takes the height above Augezd; the causeway comes under fire.
2 Dec / Allied army effectively destroyed as a field force; Russia begins withdrawing east.
26 Dec / Treaty of Pressburg: Austria cedes Venetia, Istria, Dalmatia, Tyrol and Vorarlberg.
6 Aug 1806 / Francis II abdicates as Holy Roman Emperor.

Bagration holds the height toward Rausnitz, then withdraws on Austerlitz, the Guard on Austerlitz, and the Allied left has ceased to exist as a formation.

Weyrother's dispositions send four of the five Allied columns south-west off the Pratzen plateau to turn the French right and cut the road to Vienna. Bagration holds the highway in the north, Liechtenstein's cavalry links the two, and the Russian Guard stands in reserve behind Krzenowitz. The plan assumes the French will stand still while those four columns march across their front.

Legrand's single division held roughly five kilometres of the lower Goldbach on its own. Davout's III Corps detachment, some 5,300 men in Sokolov's estimate, reached Raigern only on the night of 1 December after a forced march from Vienna, 8 km from the villages it had to hold. Against them the Allies committed roughly 38,000 to 40,000. The weakness was real, not simulated, which is what made it convincing.

Between 07:00 and 09:00 the three left-hand columns and Kienmayer's advance guard descended into the Goldbach villages and fed themselves into the fight for them. Each column that went down was a column no longer on the plateau. This map reads the Allies as having thinned the centre of their position themselves by the time Soult moved; Stutterheim and Thiébault have the 4th Column still on the plateau when the French appeared.

With the plateau taken, the Allied army was in two halves that could no longer support one another. Buxhowden's columns, roughly 38,000 to 40,000 men, were west and south of the heights; Bagration and the Guard were north and east of them. Buxhowden did not learn that the centre had gone until about noon. From this point the French hold the interior lines on their enemy's own battlefield.

The northern battle was a holding action that Lannes turned into an advance. This map reads the Santon, scarped and carrying eighteen guns, as anchoring the flank, so that Bagration could not get past it. When Liechtenstein's and Uvarov's horse charged, Murat answered with Nansouty's and d'Hautpoul's cuirassiers. Blasowitz fell, about 11:15 by this map's reckoning (no source read gives the hour); in Thiers, Lannes then carries Holubitz and Krug and parts Bagration's infantry from Liechtenstein's cavalry, while Schönhals has Bagration's battalions thrown into disorder after an attack on his left toward noon, when the Guards had given way, then gathered again, somewhat, on the height by Rausnitz.

Between about 13:00 and 14:00 Napoleon turned his centre ninety degrees and brought it down off the plateau onto the back of Buxhowden's columns, while Davout attacked from the west. Przybyszewski's column was surrounded in Sokolnitz and largely captured. The Allied left was now being attacked from the direction of its own rear.

Drafted by Gen. Franz von Weyrother, Quartermaster-General. Read aloud at Krzenowitz after midnight, in German, to an audience largely of Russian officers, with no time to copy it out.

Turn the French right with overwhelming weight, force the Goldbach at the southern villages, then wheel the left wing north-west to envelop the French as they fall back toward Brünn - severing their line to Vienna - and roll them up against the hills. The centre is to follow the attack, not hold the plateau.
That the Pratzen plateau could safely be vacated because the decisive ground was the French right.
That five columns could cross one another's lines of march in darkness and arrive in order.
Precede the 1st Column, seize Telnitz at first light, then screen the outer flank toward Menitz.
Descend from the southern plateau, force the crossing at Telnitz, then wheel north-west toward the Turas wood (the disposition's name for it).
Take Sokolnitz, cross the stream, conform on Dokhturov's right.
Take the Sokolnitz castle and the pheasantry, cross, and link the attack to the centre.
Move from Pratzen to Kobelnitz and hold the hinge between the attack and the right.
Cavalry. Cover the right of the attacking columns between Blasowitz and the plateau.
Hold the Olmütz highway, pin the French left, and link to Liechtenstein.
The Imperial Guard to remain behind Krzenowitz, in hand.
That the Allies would read the abandoned plateau and the withdrawn outposts as weakness.
That Davout could reach the lower Goldbach from Vienna in time to keep the right alive.
That Legrand could hold roughly five kilometres of stream on his own for several hours.

The risk was carried entirely on the right. In this map's interpretation, a counterfactual: if Davout had not arrived, or if Legrand had broken before nine o'clock, the bait would have been swallowed with the army behind it.
Hold the villages on the lower Goldbach and give ground slowly. Do nothing that might discourage the attack.
Saint-Hilaire behind Puntowitz, Vandamme behind Girzikowitz, out of sight in the valley. On the signal, take the Pratzeberg and Stare Vinohrady.
Climb the northern shoulder of the plateau and take the Old Vineyards, linking the assault to Lannes.
Hold the Olmütz highway with the Santon fortified and entrenched. Advance only when the centre has gone in.
Once the plateau is held from Pratzen to the highway, turn the centre ninety degrees and come down on the rear of the Allied left.

No source read calls the corps the general reserve. The 30th Bulletin gives Bernadotte the command of the centre, with Rivaud's division on his left and Drouet's on his right (p. 449); Stutterheim (1806), an Austrian officer present at the battle, writes that the corps formed the centre of the French army (p. 41); Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky has Napoleon order Bernadotte and Soult together to seize the heights of Pratzen (1846, pp. 238-239); Marbot's memoirs have the centre formed by the troops of Soult and Bernadotte (vol. I, p. 260). Thiébault's memoirs count the 2nd division of I Corps, with the Guard and the reserve, among the troops that took no part in the fighting (vol. III, p. 466; the reserve is the grenadiers' on p. 504, in a boast he imputes to Napoleon). A note in the Materialien of 1806, by its lettering one of an unnamed French officer's (an attribution read on the text layer only), has half of the corps' battalions fire no cartridge and the other half take little part (p. 93); Savary has one of its divisions break the Russian Guard's infantry (1828, pp. 205-208).
1re or 2e Div., I Corps
Gen. de division Olivier Rivaud

Its number in I Corps differs between two French returns of October 1805, neither of 2 December: the situation of 28 October numbers Rivaud's division the 2nd (Alombert and Colin, t. IV, p. 717); the force return of 26 October numbers its regiments (the 8e and 45e de ligne, the 54e detached, then under Pacthod) the 1st division, which this map reads as Rivaud's (an inference from its regiments and its brigade general). The two group the corps differently: on 26 October it also had an advance-guard division under Kellermann. Sokolov's order of battle built on the returns of 22 November has Rivaud the 1st and Drouet the 2nd (t. II, pp. 183-185). Thiébault's memoirs have I Corps' 1st division reinforce Lannes and its 2nd take no part; which of the two each is follows only from which fought, itself disputed.

IV, pp. 762 and 716-717). Sokolov's order of battle built on the returns of 22 November has it the 2nd (t. II, pp. 183-185). Russian and Soviet accounts hold that Kutuzov opposed the plan and was overruled by the Tsar; at the council itself he reportedly dozed rather than objecting. He rode with the 4th Column and was lightly wounded in the face.

Napoleon gave it up on purpose on 1 December and camped his army west of it. When the Allies marched off it in the morning he took it back with two divisions; by about 11:00 it was French from end to end and their army was split in two.
The Allies spent the morning forcing crossings that led nowhere while the battle was decided on the high ground behind them.
Przybyszewski's column was surrounded here in the afternoon and tried to break out north toward Kobelnitz. It disintegrated and surrendered almost entire.

Kollowrat and Miloradovich were ordered here from the Pratzen. They were still on the plateau when Soult arrived: held up by Liechtenstein's cavalry crossing their line of march and, in the Russian Biographical Dictionary's account (1903), chiefly by Kutuzov's reluctance to leave the heights.
The orders were read in German to an audience of largely Russian commanders, late, and with no time to distribute copies.

Positions here are reconstructed from standard accounts of the battle. Village-level locations and the sequence of attacks follow the accounts; the hours are partly dated in the sources read, partly disputed between them, and mostly this map's own, as each move's timing grade, and each event's timing and dispute, say. Exact frontages, the spacing between formations and the precise placement of cavalry reserves are not — a Napoleonic corps occupied a shifting area of ground, not a point.

Every formation marker therefore carries a confidence grade. A means the position is documented; B means the sector is documented but the frontage shown is an approximation; C means the position is reconstructed from the narrative and should be treated as indicative only.

Strengths are the hardest figures of all. The Allied column organisation split and intermingled regiments, and reputable orders of battle disagree substantially: the IV Column is about 16,100 in Schönhals's table and Sokolov's, but 23,900 in Duffy's. Where sources conflict, the dossier shows a working figure and the range.

Terrain relief is exaggerated about {EXAG} times: one map unit is {M_PER_UNIT} m on the ground, and heights follow a separate vertical scale fitted to twelve surveyed elevations (the summits and several villages), which it meets within their tolerances. Between them the drawn ground departs from today's elevation data by up to about 80 m: the southern Pratzen plateau and St Anthony's knoll are drawn 40-80 m too low and Slapanice about 45 m too high, so read heights there as approximate. At true scale the Pratzen plateau reads as a gentle rise, about 115 m from the Goldbach to the Pratzeberg over some 2.5 km. The relief setting cannot be changed while the battle plays, because redrawing the ground can take longer than a frame; the ground switch (Landscape, Paper map, Landscape with counters) can, and a slow frame while it redraws advances the battle clock by at most 1.2 minutes at 1× (4.8 at four times speed).

Villages are placed from the Czech municipality register; Turas, which it does not list, at the Czech address register's point for Tuřany, its name in Wolny's topography of 1836; Krug and Bellowitz, which no register read places, are not; summits from terrain-model data. The map keeps its historical frame, which lies about {ROT} degrees off true north. The compass rose shows true north for the current view. Raigern, Rausnitz and Kowalowitz lie beyond the frame and are shown as markers at its edge.

Open questions, left unresolved rather than guessed: the pattern of Russian infantry flags; whether Grenz infantry wore brown in 1805; whether vines stood at Telnitz and at Stare Vinohrady in 1805; the upper bound of the Russian Guard's attack; Bagration's exact line at dawn; whether the Posoritz post house stood in 1805 where the maps of 1826-52 show the post; the positions of Krug and Bellowitz, which no source read fixes; how wet the Goldbach's bottom was in December 1805 (the map draws marsh beside the lower brook from the land as recorded, not from an account of the day, which had the meres frozen); whether the Sokolnitz castle's grounds were walled and the pheasantry enclosed (neither is drawn); which of the two channels the cadastral sketch of 1825 draws north of the Sokolnitz castle carried the Goldbach in 1805 (the map draws today's, beside the avenue; the other lies about 110-150 m from it); whether the highway east of the Santon ran in 1805 where the cadastral sketches of 1826 and the survey of 1836-52 draw it, as the map draws it; Kologrivov's command of the Guard cavalry on 2 December, which Sokolov's order of battle gives, Schönhals's table only over the whole Guard and Duffy's heading only among the reserve's generals (Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky and the Chevalier Guard's history have him command the Guard cavalry at Olmütz and on the march, and the Chevalier Guard came up in Maliutin's separate column); when Blasowitz fell; when Napoleon took post on the Zuran; when Bernadotte's corps, Drouet's division with it, crossed the Goldbach; how many guns stood by the chapel of St Anthony, and whose; how many men drowned in the meres; how Suchet's and Caffarelli's divisions were numbered on the day (Suchet's the 3rd of V Corps in both October returns read, Gazan's the 2nd on 26 October; Caffarelli's, under Bisson on 28 October, the 1st of III Corps); the brigade of Gladkov, which Duffy's order of battle names and no other source read does; whether Uvarov's regiments were with Liechtenstein's column or had gone to Bagration the evening before; the numbers of Rivaud's and Drouet's divisions in I Corps, which the October returns give differently; and the hours on which the accounts read disagree with each other or with this map's timing: when the columns left the plateau (at 07:00 as the disposition ordered, the I Column at seven in Buxhowden's and Kutuzov's reports and so on the map, half past six for the left wing in Schönhals, between seven and eight in Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky; the II and III Columns at 07:30 in Schönhals, the III at 07:00 in Przybyszewski's report and the II coming down at 08:00 in Buxhowden's; all three from 07:00 on the map), when Kamensky turned his brigade about (no account read gives the hour; at 09:45 in the event, in the 08:45 phase in his brigade's record), when Rapp's counter-charge went in (by about noon in Schönhals, before one by the order of the Bulletin's narrative, about 13:00 in Rapp's and Ségur's memoirs; from 11:15 on the map), when Friant's division left Raigern (at 05:00, or between 05:30 and 06:00, in Davout's two reports, about 06:00 in Sokolov; at 05:00 on the map, with its leading brigade at the Goldbach about 09:00, as in Stutterheim and the Moniteur's remarks of 1806, and Telnitz in French hands at 09:30, then lost again, as in Davout's report), and when Bagration's corps fell back (with Blasowitz's fall on the map, 11:15; after an attack on its left toward noon in Schönhals). The map keeps its timing for Kamensky's turn, Rapp's charge and Bagration's corps. Duffy (1977) and Smith (1998), cited here for strengths, were not read. Kamensky's musketeer regiment is named here as Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky names it, Ryazhsk; the Materialien of 1806 give Ryazan, as this map earlier cited from Duffy, which is kept as the other reading. Two known limits of the terrain model are left as they are rather than reshaped to fit: its stream beds are not downhill at every point (reverse gradients of up to about 10 m within a reach), and from the chapel of St Anthony it does not show the centre of the Satschan pond, although Lejeune has Napoleon at the end on a knoll above Augezd facing the lakes, which this map takes to be the chapel's height.

Two figures on the situation line are computed from the plotted reconstruction rather than taken from a source. The holding on the heights is the sum of the strengths of formations whose plotted positions fall inside the plateau outline; because the reconstruction plots formations and not losses, a figure that does not change does not mean the fighting there has stopped. Centre separation is a spatial test, not a historical statistic: it reports whether a French formation stands across the line joining the Allied groups north and south of the plateau. When it stops being reported the geometry no longer holds, which is not the same as the Allied army having reunited.
Historical record / What the sources attest: who was there, roughly how many, which villages were attacked and when. Marked as fact in an event's dossier.

Reconstruction / How this map represents the record: a plotted position, a route between anchors, a frontage. Graded A, B or C for confidence; a formation's dossier names the grade as its position's: documented, estimated or reconstructed.

Derived reading / What the engine computes from the plot, such as the holding on the heights or the centre-separation test. Never a source figure; the holding on the heights and the centre-separation test are marked derived wherever they are shown.

Order-of-battle figures are this map's working figures, many first taken from Duffy (1977) and Smith (1998), cited and not read; where a formation's note names a source or gives what the sources read, it says so, and a figure without a note is this map's.

Narrative of the fight for the Pratzeberg draws on Thiébault's memoirs, with Schönhals and Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky where the statements name them; Duffy (1977), on which it earlier drew, was not read.
